opus-5.5.text:
I think they matter a lot, but probably not in the way people usually assume. When people talk about "race dynamics," they often treat it as a law of physics, as if there's no choice and whoever builds it first wins, so everyone has to sprint. I think that's mostly a story. It's a story that happens to be very convenient for the people doing the racing. If you're running a frontier lab and you say "we have to go fast or the bad guys will get there first," that's a wonderful justification for doing exactly what you already wanted to do.

That doesn't mean the competitive pressure isn't real. It is. Companies compete for talent, compute, and investors, and countries worry about each other. But coordination problems aren't unsolvable. We've done this before with nuclear nonproliferation, with chemical and biological weapons, with ozone-depleting chemicals. None of those were perfect, but they were far better than nothing, and they happened because enough people decided the risk was unacceptable and built institutions around that.

On misinformation, I'd frame it more broadly as epistemic pollution. The bigger problem isn't one fake video or one deceptive post. The whole information ecosystem is getting worse at letting people and governments form accurate beliefs about what's going on. If policymakers can't tell what's hype and what's real, or what's lobbying and what's genuine expertise, then good regulation becomes very hard. A lot of what reaches legislators about AI is very well-funded messaging from the people being regulated. That's a misinformation problem too, even if it's not the kind people usually mean.

So yes, both of these make regulation harder. But I resist the fatalism. "It's impossible to regulate, so don't bother" is a self-fulfilling prophecy. The public, when you actually ask them, is overwhelmingly uneasy about racing toward systems we don't understand and can't control. The political will is latent. What's missing is people willing to say plainly what's at stake and to build the institutions, like compute governance, liability, and international agreements, that make the race something you can step out of rather than something you're trapped in.

r001.rationale: It says the public is overwhelmingly uneasy about the AI race, but does not connect that support to regulation or say it remains strong despite misinformation and disinformation.

r002.rationale: It mentions countries worrying about each other, but does not say AI race dynamics pressure other countries to militarize.

r003.rationale: It supports international agreements as one way to address the race, but does not identify the absence of a treaty as allowing tensions to escalate into military conflict.

r004.rationale: It says coordination is possible and calls for institutions, but does not predict that taking more regulatory action will make subsequent action easier.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think they limit it a lot, but not in the way people usually assume. The misinformation problem isn't primarily that the public believes false things about AI. It's that the people with the most money and the most access to policymakers have an enormous incentive to muddy the water, and they're very good at it. You get this constant flood of "it's just a chatbot," "regulation will kill innovation," "China will win," and none of those claims have to be true to work. They just have to create enough uncertainty that nobody feels confident acting. That's the actual function of misinformation here. It's not persuasion, it's paralysis.

And then the race dynamics compound that, because every lab can point at every other lab and say, "Look, if we slow down, they won't." Which is a coordination problem, not a technical one. We've solved coordination problems before. We did it with nuclear testing, with CFCs, with bioweapons. Imperfectly, sure, but we did it. The difference is that in those cases the people racing eventually admitted that they were racing toward something bad. Right now you have a lot of very smart people who've convinced themselves that the race is fine, or even good, because they're the good guys and they'll get there first. Every participant in every arms race in history has believed that.

So the way I'd put it is, misinformation and race dynamics don't make regulation impossible. They make it unlikely by default. The default path is that everyone keeps going, nobody wants to be the one who blinks first, and the regulatory conversation gets captured by the incumbents writing rules that lock in their own position while doing nothing about the actual risk. Breaking out of that default requires people to say the obvious thing out loud, which is that building systems smarter than us that we don't understand and can't control is a bad idea, and we should stop doing that until we can. That's not a sophisticated position. It's just one that's very inconvenient for a lot of powerful people, and so it gets treated as fringe when it's really just common sense.

r001.rationale: The response describes misinformation as an effort by powerful interests to create uncertainty, but does not say public support for AI regulation remains strong.

r002.rationale: It discusses labs pressuring one another to keep racing, but does not argue that AI race dynamics pressure other countries to militarize.

r003.rationale: It mentions past coordination efforts, but says nothing about an absent international treaty or military conflict.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that taking more regulatory action will make further action easier.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re both serious obstacles, but I wouldn’t conclude that regulation is hopeless. The race dynamic is particularly nasty because you can have people who sincerely believe that what they’re doing is dangerous and who nevertheless keep doing it because they think, well, if we stop, somebody less responsible will get there first. And of course, everybody can tell themselves that story. It doesn’t actually establish that the outcome will be safe.

That’s one of the reasons you need regulation. You need a way for people to make commitments that are enforceable, so that being more cautious doesn’t simply mean losing to the least cautious actor. Otherwise you’re asking individual companies to solve a collective-action problem through goodwill.

Misinformation makes that harder because the public needs some reasonably accurate picture of what’s happening to demand sensible rules. But I’d distinguish deliberate misinformation from uncertainty and disagreement. We don’t understand these systems well enough to make lots of confident claims about their future capabilities. That uncertainty cuts both ways; it isn’t a justification for assuming everything will be fine.

So I think the important move is to get away from asking, ‘Do you trust this particular company?’ and toward asking, ‘What can they demonstrate, who can independently check it, and what happens if they can’t meet the standard?’ You don’t need everyone to agree on the entire future of AI to start building accountability.

r001.rationale: The response says misinformation makes it harder to demand sensible rules; it does not claim public support remains strong despite it.

r002.rationale: It describes companies continuing because they fear losing the race, but does not say race dynamics pressure countries to militarize.

r003.rationale: It mentions enforceable commitments, but says nothing about an absent international treaty or tensions escalating into military conflict.

r004.rationale: It supports starting to build accountability, but does not say that taking more regulatory action will make further action easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re major obstacles, but I don’t think they make regulation hopeless. There are two problems that reinforce each other: people disagree about what these systems can do and how dangerous they might become, and then, even when they agree there’s a risk, they say, “Well, we have to keep going because somebody else will.”

That second argument is particularly worrying because everybody can use it. Every company can point to another company, every country can point to another country, and you end up with a situation that none of the participants necessarily wants. Being ahead doesn’t, by itself, mean you know how to control what you’re building.

With misinformation, I’d distinguish deliberate deception from uncertainty and people sincerely disagreeing. We don’t need to resolve every disagreement about the future before requiring independent scrutiny, accountability, and evidence that a system is safe enough to deploy.

The point of regulation is partly to change those incentives. If doing the responsible thing means you lose your job or your company loses to a competitor, appeals to responsibility will only get you so far. You need rules that let people slow down without simply handing an advantage to whoever is least cautious. Getting that internationally is difficult. But the race dynamic is a reason to work on coordination, not a reason to give up on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses misinformation and disagreement but makes no claim about the strength of public support for AI regulation.

r002.rationale: It describes countries pointing to other countries in a race dynamic, but does not say this pressures them to militarize.

r003.rationale: It says international coordination is difficult, but does not mention an absent treaty or escalation into military conflict.

r004.rationale: It argues that regulation can change incentives and enable people to slow down, but does not say that taking more regulatory action will make later action easier.
